body.text: Children at the centre of Kununurra's crime problem can thrive given the opportunity
A boy jumps on the wreck of an old car, spins the rusty wheel, belly laughs and screeches.
Tonight he's playing on a stationary vehicle. Other nights he's driving around town.
He's one of 10 boys, mostly in their early teens, who are taking part in a trial circuit-breaker program that aims to reduce crime.
They are on the Pentecost River, fishing and joking around the fire, away from their hometown of Kununurra.
The Kimberley town, 3,000km north of Perth, is renowned for its stunning scenery of red rocky ranges and boab trees, but has been in the spotlight recently for the wrong reasons.
Drone footage of youngsters in a stolen car being chased by police was viewed millions of times when it made international headlines in July.
The wrong attention
It was the second time in less than a year Kununurra had been in the media spotlight, after a spate of youth crime in October 2025.
"You watched the news last year, miss?" a boy asks.
People working with these vulnerable children say viral videos and sensational headlines only encourage them towards dangerous acts that they also share on social media.
Each time a car theft video goes viral, media organisations parachute reporters in and extra police officers are flown into town.
But residents know youth crime is an unrelenting issue that has remained unresolved for decades.
Serious fun
Maria Bolten Magnay, a Kununurra born-and-bred business owner, says the situation has worsened over time.
"Two classmates I went to primary school with died in separate car accidents that involved stolen vehicles," she said.
"I can't believe it's happening again. It's unacceptable. The community and the victims deserve better support."
In June, a teenager with links to the East Kimberley died in an allegedly stolen car crash in Katherine, the first town you reach after leaving Kununurra and crossing the Northern Territory border.
"I was shocked … that is like, my mate," one of the boys of them says.
He says a couple of days before the crash they were in a car together.
"But the boys here, they know how to handle driving," another boy chimes in.
Asked about the potentially fatal consequences of reckless driving, it's clear most boys cannot yet fully appreciate them.
Ms Magnay says these are "not bad kids harming people with violence" but they need urgent support, as do the community members who are impacted.
She said court and detention do not seem to make a difference, citing the recent theft of her brother's car.
"They stole the car, rolled it, wrote off the car. All seven of them were injured. One child had been released from Banksia [Hill Detention Centre] the day before," she said.
"That is a big fat failure from our government."
Juvenile detention
Back at the camp, one boy who was fishing says he spent more time in detention in Perth than on country this year.
"You do it hard in Banksia," he whispers.
He says he was re-incarcerated five days after he was released.
Other boys jokingly tease him for for being arrested and sent back to Banksia Hill shortly after being released.
People working with these vulnerable children say detention is seen as a rite of passage by some.
A Youth Night Space has been touted as a solution by the state government to reduce street presence and crime, with similar centres across the north producing positive results.

While there is no opening date for the Kununurra facility, its proposed location, in the Ord agricultural precinct, opposed by a section of the community, an interim space has started operating in town.
Multiple government agencies and NGOs have attempted to tackle youth crime, with a number of programs trialled, and some discontinued.

But none have produced long-lasting solutions in the East Kimberley, one of the regions with the highest rates of juvenile offending in WA, where the minimum age of criminal responsibility is only ten.
Deep-seated issues
Jeremy Donovan, an Indigenous man with family ties to the Kimberley, works with Waringarri Aboriginal Corporation and is leading the on-country camping group.
He was incarcerated as a teenager, and can relate to the boys' experiences as a result.
"These young people at the camp, maybe 60, 70 per cent of them call me uncle, dad, grandfather, whatever it might be, and they respond to me in this way," Mr Donovan said.
"Having Indigenous-led [programs] and then [being] supported by other people is the answer."
It is not just crime that needs to be addressed in order to solve these deep-seated issues.
The camping location on the Pentecost River is the best-known crossing on famous Gibb River Road tourist route and is only an hour from Kununurra.
But many of the boys had never seen it before.
"Our kids are a symptom of the bigger picture," Mr Donovan said.
"You are not addressing poverty in this 'very lucky country'. It's not lucky for everyone.
"We have overcrowding, social dysfunctions, intergenerational trauma, historic abuse — it's all compacted and these kids are the wound of it."
Changing the narrative
Mr Donovan says the boys "are spoken about so commonly in a deficit discourse".
"'They are the problem, they are this, they are that' — out here is letting country be a reflection of how special they are," he says.
"You can already see the difference. You have 10 of the highest-offending kids, [but] my keys are in my car. I think everyone's keys are in their cars," Mr Donovan said.
The boys say if they could entertain themselves with activities other than stealing, they would do so.
"Doing these things here: fishing, going camping," one says.
A boy proudly holds up a barramundi he's just caught.
He wants it on camera, he wants people to see it — to see him, doing well.
